The conversion brought over the account master and current read but did not bring over estimate history.
On compound meters (three-inch and up, commercial accounts), the estimate logic averaged the prior twelve readings on a calendar quarter basis, while billing was done on a rolling sixty-day cycle.

Commercial accounts had estimates coming in about eleven percent light, resulting in a true-up bill of about fourteen hundred dollars in February for accounts such as 'Hillcrest Lanes,' with customers reacting by 'screaming at Doreen up front.'
Nobody caught the issue because staff were looking at the summary page.

Speaker found the pattern/issue.

Marlene read the two-page document standing up, taking about two minutes, then said, "Kovarik, you're the only one in here who actually reads the back page," put it down on the counter, and went to lunch.

Records started as a 'Green Bandy notebook' then became an Excel workbook once Excel was available on office machines, which grew to include exception logic, compound conversions, and a cross-reference for parcels resplit in annexation without new account numbers.
There are about eleven hundred parcels in that cross-reference category.

Nobody instructed speaker to create this flag.

facts.what_happened: Before working in billing, speaker worked on meters.
Worked a reading route on the west side and toward the township for two years, 1995 to 1997.
This was before radio-read technology, requiring entry into customers' basements.
Used a handheld device called the Itron and a flashlight to read meters in basements.
A woman named Ardith Bolyard, approximately 78 years old, lived on Mulberry.
Her meter read showed approximately 91,000 gallons over a sixty-day cycle; she was a widow living alone in a 1,400 square foot house.
Her normal usage was approximately 4,000 gallons.
The bill, including sewer charges billed off the water read, would have been approximately $1,100.
The specific bill amount was $1,140-something.
Speaker was 22 years old at the time.
Speaker went to the house and identified the toilet as the source.
The cause was the flapper.
The flapper was a four-dollar rubber part that had softened and was leaking silently down the back of the bowl without noise.
Ardith had not heard the leak.
Speaker went to the Hardware on Main during lunch, bought a flapper ($1.99) and a chain clip (approximately $2.40), and installed them.
The repair took eleven minutes.
Speaker recorded the meter read as a 'meter-fail estimate' in the system.
The meter had not actually failed; it was functioning correctly.
Speaker entered her twelve-month average, which processed through the system, resulting in a $41 bill; no one questioned this in thirty years.
Ardith gave speaker a can of Vernors from her refrigerator.
Speaker did not want the Vernors but drank it.

Speaker thought about the incident for about a year, then wrote a proposal on a Brother typewriter for a 'leak forgiveness' policy: a one-time adjustment to average billing for verified leaks fixed within thirty days.
This type of policy is now used by half the districts in the state and is in the current rate ordinance.
Speaker did not put his name on the typed proposal.
Speaker gave the proposal to Ron Mierzwa, saying someone might want to consider it; Ron put his own name on it.
The proposal went to the board in 1998 and passed.
Ron received a plaque, which is at his house; speaker saw it at Ron's retirement event.
Speaker states that if the proposal had carried his name as a 23-year-old meter reader, it would not have passed.
Ron had twenty-five years of tenure and golfed with a commissioner.
Ardith died sometime in the early 2000s.
Her house is now a rental with vinyl siding.
Approximately 1,100-1,200 accounts per year now go through the adjustment policy.
Speaker looked up the number once: 1,206 accounts in 2019.
Total personal cost of parts was $4.39 including the chain clip.
